title: Chapter 121 – Signal
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Jian]

Thirty days later.

They bury Mu on the ridge of the Law Pavilion, in the first week of spring, under a plain gray stone with no title.

It was Mu's own instruction. He gave it in writing, on a sheet of Court paper, three days before the Offering, and the Arbiter has read it twice to the assembled Halls in a voice that does not entirely hold. Let there be no rank on the stone. Let there be no number. Let there be the name, and the year, and the line: He chose. Shen Wuye stands now at the head of the grave in the thin sun with the paper in his hand. Beside him sit Cheng Yun, in the black of the Court, and Bai, with a plum he has not eaten, and Yuxian, and the old man from the Cloud Peak Hall who leans on his stick, and the long gray rank of the Law guards with their blades reversed.

Feng reads the Rule. It is the only part of the ceremony Mu left to a stranger. He reads Article one, the first of the Founders' words, in his slow rough voice: The Rule is a cage, and the cage is for the wolf's sake as much as the sheep's. He reads it to the end. When he closes the book there is no sound at all but the wind in the pines.

Jian stands at the back, between his mother and Ye, in a borrowed black cloak that does not fit. The Seal in his chest aches, a dull cold seam. He does not weep. He has not wept since the Gate. But when the first spadeful of earth falls on the lid, he finds that his hands, folded before him, are shaking, and his mother, without looking at him, reaches over and covers them with her own.

Qin Hao sits beside the grave on his stool, with the two gray hands in his lap. He has been carried here by four of the Law guards on a litter, and set down with great care, and he has not spoken. At the last, as the mound is rounded, he turns his head and looks at the stone, and says quietly, to no one: "Forty-one years. I had him wrong all that time. I thought he was a fool."

"He was," says Bai. "A fool and a good man. They aren't opposites."

Qin Hao almost smiles.

Kuang is there too, at the edge of the crowd, with her left arm bound across her chest and her iron bar leaning on her shoulder like a staff. She was hit three times on the Court, once through the lung. Bai says she will carry the scar for life and the cough for ten years. She has not said a word to anyone since she was carried off the stones, and she does not say one now. But when the Law guards lift their reversed blades to the sky, she lifts her bar with her good hand, and holds it there, quivering, until the last note has died.

Afterward she walks past Jian without turning her head, and drops a small object in the fold of his sleeve. It is a plain gray stone, smooth as an egg. He turns it over in his palm. On one face, scratched with a nail, are three characters: Third. Still.

He keeps it. It sits in his sleeve for the rest of the day, small and cold and entirely unremarkable, and he finds that his hand returns to it, again and again, as to a promise.

* * *

The Garden Hall takes its count that evening, as it takes it after every storm.

They sit in the long room off the cloister, on mats, with a brazier and a kettle and the smell of boiled rice. Wenyuan reads from a sheet. His voice is steady, but his spectacles have been pushed up onto his forehead, and nobody mentions it.

"Three hundred and four stood on the Court. Eleven were killed. Seven are crippled. Nineteen wounded and healing." He lays the sheet down. "We have taken in forty-one from the Zhao side, thirty from the Tan, and twelve from the lower town, who came to the gate on the third night of the siege and asked to be fed." A dry breath. "We are three hundred and ninety-six."

"Heaven," says Hu, from the corner.

"A fine clan," says Qinghe quietly. She has a cup in both hands. "Not so big as to be noticed, not so small as to be forgotten."

"We have been noticed," says Feng.

"Yes. But we have been noticed by the right people, I think." She glances at her husband. "Tell him."

Wenyuan clears his throat.

"The Pill Hall has granted us a licence," he says. "A full one. Bai signed it with his own hand, against the advice of three Elders, and he says it is the only sensible thing he has done in a decade. We may now brew and sell Rank Two medicine under the Garden Hall's own seal, without a patron." He rubs his nose. "Qinghe holds the first rank."

"I hold nothing," says Qinghe. "I only did the arithmetic."

"I broke through on the ninth day of the siege," says Wenyuan, in the same level voice. "Foundation Early. I did not tell anyone. I did not wish it said that I had done anything while my son was in the ground."

Everyone looks at him.

"Father," says Jian.

"It was a very small thing." The tall stooped man looks at his hands. "A cup of tea and a long walk. Your mother has been scolding me ever since."

Yue laughs. It is a bright, startled sound, the first in many days, and it runs round the room. Hu begins to rumble. Feng, grinning, thumps his father on the shoulder. And Jian, watching them in the lamplight, feels something in his chest loosen by a very small degree, the way a knot loosens when a hand has worked at it long enough.

They are all here, he thinks. Every one.

* * *

The Council meets on the tenth day, in the Law Pavilion, to decide what the Sect is.

It has no Head. The man who ruled it for thirty-one years still lies on a jade slab in the ridge-house under a stone with eleven Numbers sitting on it, and the Council, which has voted for eleven years by proxy, is for the first time obliged to vote with its own hands. Shen Wuye reads the Rule. Bai chews. Ye, pale and upright, says nothing. When the roll is called, the cushions fill: Pill Hall, Sutra Hall, Law Hall under an acting Elder, the Treasury under a new one, the Hall of Weights stripped of its head. The Cloud Peak Hall is led by a thin white-bearded man with a stick, who rises slowly and bows to the room.

"I have been asleep for some years," says Shen Wuping, in a voice like dry paper. "I am told a great deal has changed. I find that I agree with most of it."

There are four motions. The first is to hold the Gate as the Sect's charge under the Elder of the Stair, now and forever. It carries without dissent. The second is to name Qin Hao Elder Emeritus, and to keep the wall open to him at all hours. It carries. The third, to strike every proxy cast in the Head's name since the year of his sleeping, is moved by Ye, seconded by Shen Wuping, and carried by one vote. The fourth, to petition the ridge for the Head's release, is tabled. Nobody quite wants to say the reason.

When it is over, Yuxian waits for him on the stair of the Law Pavilion, in her sky-blue cloak, with her hands folded.

"You took the Fire," she says.

"You gave it."

"I gave it to the one who could carry it." A faint, dry smile. "I did not expect you to carry it to Purple Mansion. You are a great deal more trouble than I had been led to believe."

"My master was right?"

"My master was right about everything." Her calm eyes rest on him. "He has asked me to tell you one thing. The House will ask again. Not with a bell. Not with a seat. It will ask in a voice you cannot refuse. He thinks it will come before the year is out."

"Why?"

"Because it has lost its fire," says Yuxian. "And a thing that has lost its fire begins, at last, to feel the cold."

* * *

Pebble goes everywhere with Yue now.

She rides on the girl's shoulder in the daytime, a slate-gray loaf with a long tail, and sleeps in her satchel at night, and in the Sutra Hall's school she sits on the corner of the master's desk and corrects the apprentices' calligraphy. Her voice is small and cracked and entirely without tact. She has opinions about the Garden's soup. She has opinions about the Court. She is of the firm view that Lin Wenyuan is the only member of the family with any sense, and she makes this known in his hearing.

On the twentieth day of the recovery, Jian comes upon them in the herb beds at dusk.

Yue is on her knees in the new silver-thread with a trowel. Pebble is perched on a stone by the wall, tail curled, watching the sky go violet. They do not hear him. He stands at the end of the row with his hands in his sleeves and listens.

"—and he does not eat," Pebble is saying. "He sits there with a little gray bread and stares at the wall. It is very stupid."

"He is tired."

"He is always tired. It is his nature." A sniff. "I think it is time you told him."

Yue's trowel goes still.

"I cannot."

"You can. You have the voice and you have the hands. You are the only one he will hear." The small black eyes turn toward the girl. "He is afraid, Yue. He is more afraid than you know. He thinks the door is a door home, and it is not. It is a door out."

"Out of what?"

"I do not know." Pebble's voice drops. "That is what frightens me."

Jian steps back, quietly, behind the wall. He stands there a long time with his hand against the cold stone, listening to his sister's trowel start again, slow and careful in the earth.

* * *

Ruyan's letter comes on the twenty-fifth day, by a courier in the Tan colors, sealed with the jade ring.

It is short. It is written in her cramped, upright, ink-stained hand, and it says that the southern road is open, that the Associate House of Tan has lost four caravans and gained nine, and that Cloud Peak's quiet stranglehold on the Garden's goods has collapsed in a month of weeping debtors. It says that her uncle Boren has begun to talk. It says that she has found in his accounts a ledger of forty-one names, and that she has given it, as she promised, to the Gate Bearer's Court, and not to the House.

I do not know what you did, she writes. I know only that every Number in the lower town came to me at the same hour on the same morning, asking for a place to hide. I told them the Garden Hall takes in the lost. I am told you are a man who does not turn away the lost. I hope this is true.

Sixty silver a month, she adds, at the end. It was never the money. It was the habit. Tell Feng that the Tan niece is nineteen, and likes swords, and has asked twice about him.

He reads it twice in the cloister, in the evening light, and laughs aloud, and then stops, because the sound of it surprises him.

* * *

On the twenty-eighth day he takes Ye to the ridge.

She asks for nothing. She comes to the foot of the Dock stair at dawn in her old gray cloak, with her stick wrapped in cloth, and says: "I wish to see where she sat." He does not ask who. They climb the nine hundred steps in silence, up through the pines and the thinning snow, to where the ridge-house stands under its black eaves with a pale slab laid across its door and eleven men in plum sitting on it, motionless, in the cold.

They do not rise. They do not speak. They only turn their heads as the two climbers come into the clearing, and Jian sees, in the lacquer of the nearest mask, the small bent shape of an old woman with a stick.

"Teacher," says Ye.

It is a whisper. It carries.

The nearest Number sits very still. Then it lifts one gloved hand and, slowly, as one might lay down a heavy thing, points to the left of the house, to a narrow path winding up between the pines to a little shelter of boards. A small gray figure is standing at its door, in a plain wool robe, bareheaded in the snow. She is very old. She is very thin. She holds a black walnut-wood stick in her hand, the twin of Ye's, and she does not move.

Ye goes forward alone.

He stays where he is, in the clearing, with eleven Numbers on a stone and the wind in the pines. He does not watch. He watches the stone. But he hears, across the snow, in a voice he has never heard from the Elder of the Sutra Hall, a sound that is not a word at all, and then a second voice, thin and dry and broken, saying a name that is not Ye's. A name that is older. A name that is a small bright bird.

He turns his back and counts the pines until it is quiet.

* * *

Qin Hao is waiting for him on the stair the night before, on his stool, in the lamplight.

He has been carried there by two Law guards at his own insistence, and set down in front of the open wall with his stone hands resting in his lap, and he has been sitting there since dusk like a very old, very patient piece of the Gate itself. When Jian stops in front of him, the old man does not look up.

"The stone is restless," he says.

"Elder?"

"I can hear it now. It is not a great talker. It says a word or two at dusk, when the wind drops." The dry voice is almost fond. "It says the same thing, over and over. A name. I thought at first it was yours."

"What name?"

"Cole." Qin Hao turns his head slowly. His eyes are clear and unafraid. "It said it eight times last night. Eight times, boy. One for each of them. It is counting. I do not think it knows how to stop."

Jian says nothing. The wind moves in the pines.

"I will not ask what it means," says the old man. "I have been the Elder of the Stair for sixty-three years, and I have learned that some doors are better left to the one with the key. But I wish you to know that whatever is down there, you do not go down alone." He lifts one gray hand an inch, in a gesture that was once a blessing. "The wall will open when you ask. It will close behind you when you ask. And while I live, no one comes through it who is not called."

"Thank you."

"Do not thank me. Go and sleep." A pause. "And boy."

"Yes?"

"Whatever the voice says. Whatever it is. You are not obliged to believe it." The old man's mouth moves. "I have found that to be a great comfort."

* * *

On the thirtieth day the Seal is whole, and the Dock opens its eyes.

He goes down alone at dawn, as he has gone down every dawn for nine years, with the stair-light at his back. The door at the bottom accepts his palm. The air smells of stone and cold lamp-oil. The bench waits, the register waits, the long gray table waits with the pale blue bowl at its center, empty now, a cup without a fire. He sits in the stone chair. He rests his hands on his knees.

He says, "Status."

```
OPERATOR ARK-7 :: STATUS
CE: 15 / RESERVOIR 43.
SEAL: 71% (HEALING). CRACK: SEALED. RECOVERY COMPLETE IN 12 DAYS.
QI: PURPLE MANSION (9). BODY: FOUNDATION PEAK (8). SOUL: FOUNDATION PEAK (8).
OPERATOR LEVEL: 2.
FRAGMENTS: 1 (SEATED, TIER 2), 2 (SEATED, TIER 2), 3 (SHELF, UNSEATED).
LONG RELAY: OPEN. MESSAGE WAITING FOR 30 DAYS.
READ?
```

He had known it would be there. It has been there since the morning of the Gate, a small cold presence at the edge of his mind. He has not asked. He has waited, as a man waits to open a letter from a physician. He has told himself he was waiting for his hands to stop shaking.

Before he reads it he asks one question more, because he must.

```
QUERY: OPERATOR LEVEL 2 NOW. CAN THE DOOR IN THE SOUL VESSEL BE OPENED?
RESULT: YES. CONSENT OBTAINED. SEAL REQUIRED: 80% OR HIGHER.
CURRENT SEAL: 71%.
NOTE: THE MESSAGE SHOULD BE READ FIRST.
NOTE: THIS IS A RECOMMENDATION FROM THE AUTHOR OF THE DOOR.
```

From the author of the door. He reads the line twice, and a small cold finger runs down his spine.

He lets the quiet go on for a minute more.

Then he says, "Read."

* * *

The wall brightens.

It does not write. It shows. The long gray panel of the Dock goes smooth, and then pale, and then a surface appears on it that he has not seen in thirty-six years: a sheet of lined paper, slightly crumpled, with a ragged edge where it was torn from a spiral binding. It is photographed from above, in a flat white light, as if laid on a desk. In the corner of the frame lies the edge of a pen: a blue plastic pen, chewed at the cap.

The writing is in blue ink.

He knows it.

He knows it before he has read a word. He knows the lean, backward-leaning hand with the long tails on the y's and the way the t's are crossed too high. He has seen that hand once, years ago, on the back of a small cardboard tag, in a dream. He has seen it in the mirror of memory, signing a form at the foot of a long bright corridor, and he has seen it on the inner lid of his own skull when he lies awake. It is the handwriting of a man named Ethan Cole.

It is his handwriting.

Ethan —

If ARK-3 has shown you this, then the keys are in your hands and the Gate is at the door, and you have forgotten why we did it. I am sorry. I made you forget. It was the only way you would be honest with them.

Do not go through. Not yet. Whatever they offer, whatever she says, make them say the cost out loud.

Ask her where the Operators went.

Ask Lan Tong what "home" means. Ask it twice.

I left one thing in your soul. The door has your name on it because I put it there. It is not a trap. It is not a gift. Open it when the Seal is whole and you are no longer afraid.

You will not like what is behind it. I did not.

— E.C.

(the first one)

He reads it once.

He reads it again, slowly, the way a man reads a sentence in a language he used to speak.

The first one.

The Dock is very still. The lamp burns. Beside him, in its empty bowl, the ghost of the gold fire makes a faint dry ticking sound, as a cooling stone does. Somewhere above, through forty feet of rock and wall, a bell is beginning to ring for the morning meal.

He lifts one hand and holds it before his eyes. He turns it. The scarred gray skin. The long fingers. The faint ridge of a callus where the brush rests. He tries, very carefully, to remember writing anything at all, a letter, a list, a signature, with a blue plastic pen on a sheet of lined paper, and cannot. There is nothing there. There is only the clean place where the memory ought to be, smooth as a cut.

I made you forget.

"Who," he says aloud, and his voice is a stranger's, "wrote this?"

The register does not answer at once. When it does, it speaks in its dry, patient, impersonal way, as it has spoken for nine years, and the words are quite plain.

```
QUERY: AUTHOR OF MESSAGE.
RESULT: COLE, ETHAN.
QUERY: IS COLE, ETHAN THE OPERATOR?
RESULT: YES.
QUERY: WHICH OPERATOR?
RESULT: RESTRICTED. OPERATOR LEVEL 2 PERMITS ONE VIEW.
CONFIRM VIEW OF OPERATOR ROLL (SEVEN PRIOR ENTRIES)?
```

His mouth is dry. He knows he should wait. He knows what the note said. Make them say the cost out loud. But the cost is here, in the room, and it will not be made to wait.

"Confirm," he says.

The panel changes. A column of names comes up, small and plain and numbered, in the oldest script. Each has a date of arrival and a date of ending. Each has a note in a field marked CAUSE. The first is a long time ago. The last is thirty-five years.

He reads them from the top.

OPERATOR 1. COLE, ETHAN. ARRIVED: BEFORE THE ROLL. ENDED: BEFORE THE ROLL. CAUSE: GATE (INCOMPLETE).

OPERATOR 2. COLE, ETHAN. ARRIVED: YEAR 46. ENDED: YEAR 52. CAUSE: GATE (INCOMPLETE).

OPERATOR 3. COLE, ETHAN.

OPERATOR 4. COLE, ETHAN.

OPERATOR 5. COLE, ETHAN.

OPERATOR 6. COLE, ETHAN.

OPERATOR 7. COLE, ETHAN. ARRIVED: YEAR 410. ENDED: YEAR 461. CAUSE: GATE (INCOMPLETE).

And below that, in a line of its own, in a script a little brighter than the rest, as though it had been written only this morning:

OPERATOR 8. COLE, ETHAN. ARRIVED: YEAR 461. STATUS: ACTIVE.

He sits in the stone chair for a very long time, with his scarred hands open on his knees and the cold light of the Dock lying on his face. He does not move. He does not breathe. Behind the dome, deep in the rock, the great patient machine hums on, as it has hummed for six hundred years.

He thinks of a woman in a brown shawl who said, This one is not for here. He thinks of a lamp that burned blue for nine breaths. He thinks of an old man in a pavilion who said, The House cannot take. It can only be given. He thinks of Lan Tong, sitting on the lip of a basin, saying, Lin Jian does not follow.

And he thinks of a line of blue ink on a sheet of lined paper, leaning backward, with the t's crossed too high.

(the first one)

Seven men have come to the Gate and died. Seven men with one name. And an eighth sits in a stone chair under a mountain with a note in his own hand, and a door in his soul that bears the name he cannot remember, and a long relay that is open, and silent, and waiting.

If every Operator was Ethan Cole, he thinks, then which of us is the one who is going home?

And the lamp in the Dock burns steadily on, and nothing answers.
